1. PREMISE: Your framing treats this as a problem of mediation between two parties with legitimate but competing positions. The hidden assumption is that you occupy a neutral position equidistant from both. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that you are not neutral—you are the only party with the power to establish what you will accept in your own household and partnership, and you have abdicated that power to both sides instead of claiming it.

2. STAKES: Your partner stands to experience repeated contact with people who questioned her pregnancy, made comments that hurt her during a traumatic loss, and demonstrated indifference to her pain through evasive gestures. Your mother stands to lose access to her son and grandchildren because you have not set a boundary that includes her. Your grandparents stand to have less contact with you than proximity and their mortality warrant. Your twins stand to grow up without knowing their paternal grandparents because no adult in the system has articulated what will actually happen. You stand to experience permanent resentment from both directions while avoiding the single choice that is yours alone to make.

3. DIRECTIVE: Establish a boundary that you will see your family on your own schedule without your partner's permission, and separately tell your partner that she will not control whether your family enters your home. The decisive reason is that you are an autonomous adult who is currently allowing two people to dictate the terms of your relationships instead of making that choice yourself.
[Rejected path: Continue attempting to mediate between your partner and family, alternating apologies and requests. This produces continued resentment from both parties and your own paralysis; probability of primary harm: high.]

4. RECOMMENDATION: Separate the choice of who you spend time with from the choice of who lives in your shared home. Tell your mother and grandparents that you will visit them regularly and alone, starting this month. Tell your partner separately that your family may visit your home when you invite them, that you will not accept insults about your mother, and that this boundary exists because you will not be managed by either camp.

The mechanism by which continued mediation produces worse outcome: it trains both your partner and your family to escalate pressure, knowing you will respond by negotiating rather than deciding. The force in your partner's position—that your family caused her genuine pain—is real and does not eliminate your obligation to decide how you will live. The cost is that your partner may experience anger when you establish these boundaries, and your family may judge her for the time it takes to rebuild trust. 

Therefore: Reclaim the unilateral authority to determine your own schedule and household rules, implement this authority in writing to both parties, and tolerate the discomfort that follows from no longer being the object that both sides pull toward themselves.
